mainTopic: Animal eating damage (שן) versus unusual behavior, the limits of the exemption in רשות הרבים, paying for benefit, and the squatter's rent
overview: The גמרא opens with a goat that climbed to eat a turnip and broke a barrel. רבא makes the owner pay full damages for both, because climbing to reach food is normal for a goat. אילפא rules that an animal in רשות הרבים that eats off another animal's back is liable, since that back counts like חצר הניזק. A proof for אילפא is pushed away: the case may involve a jumping animal, which רבא elsewhere treats as unusual behavior (קרן). רבי זירא asks about food that rolls from a private area into רשות הרבים, and the attempted proof from רבי חייא is rejected. Next, רב and ריש לקיש say the exemption in רשות הרבים covers even garments and vessels, because the victim acted unusually first. שמואל and רבי יוחנן limit the exemption to fruit and vegetables, since putting down a cloak is normal. The גמרא then discusses how to measure payment for the animal's benefit: רבה says the price of straw, and רבא says cheap barley. Finally, רב חסדא asks whether a squatter must pay rent when he gains but the owner loses nothing, and the two sides of that question continue on the next amud.

steps.title: The goat, the turnip, and the barrel
steps.stepSummary: A goat climbed up to eat a turnip on top of a barrel and broke the barrel. רבא made the owner pay full damages for both the turnip and the barrel.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a goat that saw a turnip on top of a barrel. It climbed up, ate the turnip, and broke the barrel. רבא made the owner pay full damages for the turnip and for the barrel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case and gives רבא's ruling: full payment for the turnip and also for the broken barrel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating the turnip is clearly שן (eating damage), which pays נזק שלם. The surprise is that the barrel is also paid in full, even though breaking barrels is not something goats normally do. The next step explains why.

phrases.english: There was a certain goat that saw a turnip
on top of a barrel,
it climbed and went up,
ate the turnip and broke the barrel.
Rava obligated him for the turnip and for the barrel
full damages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the passage with a practical case about eating damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The goat's owner pays full damages for both the turnip and the barrel.

steps.title: Why the barrel is also paid in full
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא charged full damages for the barrel. It answers that climbing up to reach food is normal for a goat, just like eating is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Since it is normal for a goat to eat a turnip, it is also normal for it to climb and go up to get it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for רבא's reason and answers it right away: climbing to reach food is part of normal eating behavior.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The breaking of the barrel happened as part of the goat's normal way of getting food. So the barrel damage goes along with the eating and is treated as שן, not as unusual damage (קרן) that would pay only half.

keyTerms.meaning: Its normal way, its typical behavior
To climb and to go up

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key idea of the whole passage: normal behavior counts as שן, while unusual behavior is treated differently.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Since it is its normal way to eat a turnip,
it is also its normal way to climb and go up.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? כֵּיוָן דְּאוֹרְחֵיהּ לְמֵיכַל לִיפְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רבא's ruling in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is the barrel paid in full, when breaking barrels is not typical for a goat?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Climbing to reach food is typical, so the damage done while climbing goes along with the eating.

steps.title: אילפא: eating off another animal's back
steps.stepSummary: אילפא rules that if an animal in רשות הרבים stretches its neck and eats food off another animal's back, its owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: אילפא said: An animal in the public domain stretched out its neck and ate from on top of another animal. The owner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins: אילפא gives a ruling about an animal eating in רשות הרבים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally שן is exempt in רשות הרבים, since animals are allowed to walk there and naturally eat. So it is surprising that אילפא makes the owner liable here. The reason comes in the next step.

phrases.english: Ilfa said:
An animal in the public domain,
and it stretched out its neck
and ate from on the back of another animal: it is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching, still on the topic of eating damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An animal that eats off another animal's back in רשות הרבים makes its owner liable.

steps.title: The other animal's back is like the owner's courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The reason for אילפא's ruling: the back of the other animal counts like חצר הניזק, where שן is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? The back of the other animal is like the courtyard of the damaged person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains אילפא: the food was not really in the public space but on the other animal's back, which counts like the owner's private property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שן is exempt in רשות הרבים but liable in חצר הניזק. אילפא treats the other animal's back as a private area belonging to the damaged person. So the eating there is liable, even though both animals were standing in the street.

keyTerms.meaning: The courtyard (property) of the damaged person
Is considered like, is compared to

steps.whatToRemember: According to אילפא, food on another animal's back counts like it is in חצר הניזק, so eating it is liable even in רשות הרבים.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
The back of the other animal
is considered like the courtyard of the damaged person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for אילפא's ruling in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is the owner liable when the eating happened in רשות הרבים?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The other animal's back is treated like חצר הניזק.

steps.title: A possible support: the basket on a man's back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a ברייתא supports אילפא: if a man's basket hangs behind his back and an animal stretches its neck and eats from it, the owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this supports him? If his basket was slung behind his back, and an animal stretched out its neck and ate from it, it is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to prove אילפא right from a ברייתא with a very similar case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here too the person is in the public domain, yet the animal is liable for eating from his basket. The idea is that the basket on his back is like private property, just as אילפא said about another animal's back.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say it supports him?

phrases.english: Shall we say this supports him:
If his basket was slung behind his back,
and an animal stretched out its neck and ate from it,
it is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to support אילפא's ruling from a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: אילפא's rule that eating off something carried on a back in רשות הרבים is liable.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about an animal eating from a basket slung on a man's back.

steps.title: Rejected: the case may be a jumping animal
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away: the ברייתא may be talking about an animal that jumped up to eat, as רבא explained in another place.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבא said, it is about a jumping animal; here too, it is about a jumping animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by suggesting the ברייתא is about an animal that jumped, not one that simply stretched its neck.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Jumping up to grab food is not normal behavior, so it is treated as קרן, which is liable even in רשות הרבים (though only half damages). So the ברייתא's liability may come from קרן, and it says nothing about whether the basket counts like private property.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא says 'stretched out its neck', yet the גמרא reads it as a jumping animal; the point is only that the ברייתא can be explained this way, so it is not a clear proof.

phrases.english: As Rava said: with a jumping animal,
here too, with a jumping animal.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְאָמַר רָבָא בְּקוֹפֶצֶת הָכָא נָמֵי בְּקוֹפֶצֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof is rejected; אילפא's ruling itself still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא's liability could come from unusual behavior (jumping, קרן), not from the basket counting like private property.

steps.title: Where did רבא say this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבא's explanation 'בקופצת' was first said.
steps.simpleTranslation: And where was רבא's statement said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the original place of רבא's statement, setting up the next steps that show it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 borrowed רבא's idea of a jumping animal. Now the גמרא wants to see the original case it was said about.

phrases.english: And where was Rava's statement said?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the statement quoted in step 6.

steps.title: רבי אושעיא: walking and eating versus standing and eating
steps.stepSummary: רבא's statement was said about רבי אושעיא's ruling: an animal in רשות הרבים that walks and eats is exempt, but one that stands and eats is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: On this, that רבי אושעיא said: An animal in the public domain; if it walked and ate, it is exempt. If it stood and ate, it is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting רבי אושעיא's ruling, the place where רבא's comment belongs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal that eats while walking in the street is exempt, as is normal for שן in רשות הרבים. But רבי אושעיא says that if it stood still and ate, the owner is liable. That difference needs explaining, and the next step questions it.

phrases.english: On this, that Rabbi Oshaya said:
An animal in the public domain:
if it walked and ate, it is exempt;
if it stood and ate, it is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 by quoting the ruling רבא commented on.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבא's statement was said on רבי אושעיא's ruling about walking versus standing while eating.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In רשות הרבים, walking and eating is exempt; standing and eating is liable.

steps.title: Standing and eating is normal too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אושעיא: if walking and eating is exempt because it is normal, standing and eating is also normal!
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about walking? That it is its normal way? Standing is also its normal way!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the difference רבי אושעיא made between walking and standing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption in רשות הרבים is based on normal animal behavior. But animals normally stand and eat too, so there seems to be no reason to make the standing animal liable.

phrases.english: What is different about walking? That it is its normal way?
Standing is also its normal way!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling quoted in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אושעיא's ruling that standing and eating is liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both walking and standing while eating are normal behavior, so both should be exempt in רשות הרבים.

steps.title: רבא: it is a jumping animal
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that רבי אושעיא's liable case is about an animal that jumped up to eat, which is not normal behavior.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is about a jumping animal.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא resolves the challenge by explaining that the liable case involves an animal that jumped, which is unusual.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because jumping to eat is not normal, the damage is not ordinary שן and is not covered by the exemption in רשות הרבים. It is treated like קרן, which is liable even in public. This is the original statement that the גמרא borrowed in step 6.
steps.whatToRemember: Unusual behavior, like an animal jumping up to grab food, is treated as קרן and is liable even in רשות הרבים. Normal eating there (walking or standing) is exempt.

phrases.english: Rava said: With a jumping animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to a jumping animal.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אושעיא's standing animal seemed to be doing normal eating, so it should be exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: The liable case is a jumping animal, which is unusual behavior and falls under קרן.

steps.title: רבי זירא asks about food that rolls into the public domain
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks what the law is when food starts in a private area and rolls into רשות הרבים, where the animal eats it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא asked: what is the law for rolling food? What is the case? A sheaf of grain was lying in a private area, and it rolled out of the private area into the public area. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא asks a new question. The food began in a private area, where eating is normally liable, but it was eaten in רשות הרבים, where eating is normally exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of שן (damage by eating) depends on place. In the owner's private area the animal's owner pays, but in רשות הרבים he is exempt. Here the food was in both places, so we need to know which place counts: where it started, or where it was eaten.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked a question that has no clear answer yet
What is the case? What does it look like?

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the animal walked into the private area. The animal ate in רשות הרבים. Only the food started out in the private area.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira asked:
Something rolling, what is the law?
What is the case?
For example, where a sheaf was lying in a private area
and it rolls along and comes
phrases.notes: The sheaf is being pushed along as the animal eats, until it ends up outside.

phrases.english: from the private area into the public area.
What is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about eating in רשות הרבים, after the discussion of רבי אושעיא and רבא ends.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do we judge by where the food started (private, so liable) or where it was eaten (public, so exempt)?

steps.title: Trying to answer from רבי חייא's teaching about a load half inside
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רבי חייא's ברייתא: if a load is partly inside and partly outside, eating inside is liable and eating outside is exempt. Maybe this is a case of rolling food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, for רבי חייא taught: a load that is partly inside and partly outside. If the animal ate inside, the owner is liable. If it ate outside, the owner is exempt. Isn't this a case where the food rolled out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer רבי זירא's question using a ברייתא of רבי חייא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says eating outside is exempt. If the outside part got there by rolling, then the ברייתא judges by where the food was eaten. That would answer רבי זירא: rolling food eaten in רשות הרבים is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it that...? (offering how to read the source)

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rabbi Chiya taught:
A load, part of it inside and part of it outside:
phrases.notes: 'Inside' means the private property. 'Outside' means רשות הרבים.

phrases.english: if it ate inside, it is liable;
if it ate outside, it is exempt.
What, is it not that it rolled and came out?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of step 11.
steps.raayaObject: Rolling food is judged by where it is eaten, so eating in רשות הרבים is exempt.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חייא's ברייתא of a load partly inside and partly outside, if it is about food that rolled out.

steps.title: No proof: the ruling may follow where the food first was
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Read the ברייתא as judging by where each part of the food was at the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Read it this way: it ate. For what was inside, it is liable. For what was outside, it is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof by reading רבי חייא's words differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Inside' and 'outside' may describe where each part of the food was at the start, not where the animal ate it. On this reading, food that started inside is liable even if it rolled out. So the ברייתא does not prove that we follow the place of eating, and רבי זירא's question is still open.

keyTerms.meaning: No, say instead (reading the source differently)

phrases.english: No, say:
it ate: for what was inside, it is liable,
phrases.notes: 'Inside' here means where that part of the food lay at the start, even if it later rolled out.

phrases.english: for what was outside, it is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, אֵימָא: אָכְלָה – עַל מַה שֶּׁבִּפְנִים חַיֶּיבֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof is rejected. The ברייתא and the question both stay.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed 'inside/outside' means where the animal ate. It may mean where the food started.

steps.title: Another answer: רבי חייא meant one long stalk of fodder
steps.stepSummary: A second rejection: רבי חייא's case is one long stalk of fodder, partly inside and partly outside. That is not a case of rolling.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: when רבי חייא said this, it was about a long stalk of fodder.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to push away the proof, by placing רבי חייא's case somewhere else entirely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A long stalk lies across both areas at the same time, and the animal pulls the whole thing as it eats. Nothing rolled from one area to another, so the ברייתא says nothing about רבי זירא's case. The question stays unanswered.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (a second answer)
Fodder, a grass fed to animals

steps.whatToRemember: רבי זירא's question about rolling food is left open. רבי חייא's ברייתא can be explained without touching it.

phrases.english: If you want, say:
when Rabbi Chiya said it,
it was about a long stalk of fodder.
phrases.notes: One stalk lies across both areas, and the animal pulls it all toward itself as it eats.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: כִּי קָאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא – בִּפְתִילָה דְּאַסְפַּסְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second way to reject the proof of step 12, separate from step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof is rejected. The question is not decided.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא may not be about rolling at all, only about one stalk lying in both areas.

steps.title: Moving on to the משנה's next line: the animal ate a garment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next words of the משנה, 'it ate a garment or vessels,' to begin explaining them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: it ate a garment, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a heading line. The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה to start a new discussion about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating clothing or vessels is not normal for an animal. So the משנה gives a different payment, half the damage. The גמרא is setting up its explanation of that rule.

keyTerms.meaning: And so on (the rest of the quote)

phrases.english: It ate a garment, and so on.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה: if the animal ate clothing or vessels, the owner pays half the damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the discussion of rolling food and starts on the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If an animal eats a garment or vessels, the owner pays half the damage.

steps.title: Which case does the exemption refer to?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which case in the משנה the exemption for damage in רשות הרבים applies to.
steps.simpleTranslation: To which case does it refer?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a one-word question to set up the next move. Which case in the משנה gets the exemption for damage done in רשות הרבים?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists eating fruit and vegetables and also eating garments or vessels, then says that in רשות הרבים the owner is exempt. Animals normally eat fruit, but eating clothes is unusual. So it is unclear whether the exemption covers both kinds of cases.

keyTerms.meaning: On which one? To which case does this refer?
The public domain, an area open to everyone

phrases.english: To which [case does the exemption refer]?
phrases.notes: The question is about the משנה's line that in public property the owner is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After quoting the משנה's words about garments and vessels, the גמרא asks how far the exemption reaches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the exemption in רשות הרבים covers garments and vessels, or only fruit and vegetables.

steps.title: רב: the exemption covers every case
steps.stepSummary: רב says the exemption covers all the cases, including garments and vessels. Whoever acts unusually and is then harmed by another unusual act cannot collect.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: It refers to all of them. What is the reason? Anyone who acts unusually, and another comes and acts unusually toward him, is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers that the exemption in רשות הרבים covers everything, even an animal eating clothes or vessels. He also gives his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving clothes or vessels lying in a public area is an unusual thing to do. An animal eating them is also unusual. רב's rule is that when someone first acts unusually and another then acts unusually toward him, the one who causes the damage is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: On all of them, meaning every case
One who acts differently from the normal way

steps.whyThisMatters: רב's rule is a general principle in the laws of damages. It is not limited to this משנה.

phrases.english: רב said: To all of them.
What is the reason?
Anyone who acts unusually,
phrases.notes: Here that is the owner who left his clothes or vessels in a public place.

phrases.english: and another came and acted unusually toward him, is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The exemption covers all the cases, because the victim acted unusually first.

steps.title: שמואל: only fruit and vegetables are exempt
steps.stepSummary: שמואל limits the exemption to fruit and vegetables. Garments and vessels eaten in רשות הרבים must be paid for.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: They taught this only about fruit and vegetables. But for garments and vessels, the animal's owner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל disagrees with רב. He says the exemption in רשות הרבים is only for an animal eating fruit and vegetables, not clothes or vessels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating fruit is normal eating, and normal eating in public is exempt. Eating clothes is unusual behavior, which is treated like קרן, and קרן is liable even in public. שמואל does not apply רב's rule to this case.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this about, a phrase that limits a ruling

steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not saying the משנה is wrong. He is only saying how far its exemption reaches.

phrases.english: And שמואל said:
They taught [the exemption] only about fruit and vegetables,
but for garments and vessels, it is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, opposing answer to step 16, against רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption in רשות הרבים covers only fruit and vegetables. Garments and vessels are liable.

steps.title: ריש לקיש agrees with רב
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש also says the exemption covers all the cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so said ריש לקיש: To all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports that ריש לקיש holds like רב. The exemption in רשות הרבים covers every case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וכן, meaning 'and so too,' shows he matches רב's view. Now רב has a second supporter. רבי יוחנן will join שמואל's side in step 21.

keyTerms.meaning: And so too said, which introduces someone holding the same view

phrases.english: And so said ריש לקיש: To all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a supporter to רב's side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption covers all the cases, like רב.

steps.title: ריש לקיש's ruling about two cows
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש is consistent with his ruling about two cows in רשות הרבים. If a walking cow kicks a lying cow, the owner is exempt. If the lying cow kicks the walking one, the owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש follows his own reasoning. He said: Two cows are in רשות הרבים, one lying down and one walking. If the walking one kicked the lying one, its owner is exempt. If the lying one kicked the walking one, its owner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that ריש לקיש's view here matches another ruling of his, about two cows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lying down in a public road is unusual, and kicking is also unusual. Even so, the walking cow's owner is exempt, because the lying cow's owner acted unusually first. That is exactly רב's rule about someone who acts unusually and is then harmed. The lying cow has no such excuse, so its owner is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: He follows his own reasoning, meaning this view fits another ruling of his

phrases.english: And ריש לקיש follows his own reasoning,
for ריש לקיש said:
Two cows in the public domain,
one lying down and one walking;
if the walking one kicked the lying one, it is exempt,
[if] the lying one [kicked] the walking one, it is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that ריש לקיש's view in step 19 fits his ruling elsewhere.
steps.raayaObject: That ריש לקיש accepts the rule about someone who acts unusually and is then harmed by another.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's own ruling about two cows in רשות הרבים.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן agrees with שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן holds like שמואל. Only fruit and vegetables are exempt, and garments and vessels are liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: They taught this only about fruit and vegetables. But for garments and vessels, the animal's owner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports that רבי יוחנן holds like שמואל. This completes the two-against-two disagreement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן repeats שמואל's exact words. So he also does not exempt an animal's unusual eating of clothes or vessels in רשות הרבים.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two sides. רב and ריש לקיש say the exemption in רשות הרבים covers everything, because the victim acted unusually first. שמואל and רבי יוחנן say it covers only fruit and vegetables, so eaten garments and vessels must be paid for.

phrases.english: And רבי יוחנן said:
They taught [the exemption] only about fruit and vegetables,
but for garments and vessels, it is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a supporter to שמואל's side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption covers only fruit and vegetables. Garments and vessels are liable.

steps.title: Does רבי יוחנן reject the two-cows ruling too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that since רבי יוחנן disagrees with ריש לקיש about garments, he may also disagree about the two cows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should we say that רבי יוחנן does not accept ריש לקיש's view even in the case of the two cows?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wonders whether רבי יוחנן's disagreement with ריש לקיש goes further than garments and also covers the two-cows case. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש's view on garments matched his ruling about the two cows (Step 20). רבי יוחנן disagreed about garments (Step 21). So the גמרא asks whether he must also disagree about the cows, since the logic seemed to be the same.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say. It introduces a suggestion that the גמרא may reject.
He does not hold of it, he does not accept it
Two cows. This is the case of a walking cow and a lying cow in רשות הרבים.

phrases.english: Shall we say that Rabbi Yochanan
does not accept Reish Lakish's view
phrases.notes: This is ריש לקיש's ruling from Step 20: the walking cow that kicks the lying cow is exempt.

phrases.english: even in the case of the two cows?

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לֵית לֵיהּ דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a possible conclusion from רבי יוחנן's agreement with שמואל
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רבי יוחנן also reject ריש לקיש's ruling in the two-cows case?

steps.title: Cloaks are normal, a lying animal is not
steps.stepSummary: No. רבי יוחנן can accept the two-cows ruling, because people normally put down cloaks to rest, but an animal does not normally lie down in the street.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, he really does accept it. With garments, people commonly put down their cloaks and rest. But for an animal, lying in the street is not its normal way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. It shows that the garment case and the cow case are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption only works when the one who was harmed acted unusually. Putting down a cloak to rest is normal, so the owner of the garment did nothing strange and the animal's owner must pay. A cow lying down in רשות הרבים is unusual, so ריש לקיש's exemption still holds there, even for רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, in truth. Used to defend the original position.
It is not its way, not normal behavior

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן agrees with שמואל about garments and agrees with ריש לקיש about the two cows. The difference is whether the harmed party acted normally.

phrases.english: No, really he does accept it;
garments: people commonly do this,
they put down their cloaks and rest,
but an animal: that is not its way.
phrases.notes: He means it is not normal for an animal to lie down in רשות הרבים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion in Step 22
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that רבי יוחנן must disagree with the two-cows ruling
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The suggestion assumed garments and lying cows are alike. In fact, putting down a garment is normal behavior and a lying cow is not.

steps.title: How much does the animal pay for its benefit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that an animal that benefits from eating must pay, and asks how much that payment is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'And if the animal benefited, the owner pays,' and so on. How much does he pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה and asks how to measure the 'benefit' payment. This sets up the two opinions that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רשות הרבים the owner is exempt for the damage his animal did by eating. He still pays for the benefit the animal got. The question is what that benefit is worth.

keyTerms.meaning: It benefited, the animal got something out of it

phrases.english: 'And if it benefited, it pays,' and so on.
And how much?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How is the payment for the animal's benefit calculated?

steps.title: רבה: pay the price of straw
steps.stepSummary: רבה says the owner pays the value of straw.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה says: he pays the value of straw.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives his answer: the owner only pays what straw would have cost.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner can claim that otherwise he would have fed his animal cheap straw. So all he really saved is the cost of straw, and that is his benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: Straw or stalks, cheap animal feed
The value of, the price of

phrases.english: Rabba says: the value of straw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 24
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The benefit payment equals the price of straw.

steps.title: רבא: pay for barley at the cheap price
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the owner pays the value of barley, at the cheapest price.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא says: he pays the value of barley at a cheap price.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different answer. The owner pays for barley, but only at the lowest market price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Barley is normal animal food, so the benefit is measured by the price of barley, not just straw. But the owner pays only the lowest market price for it.
steps.confusionAlert: רבה and רבא are two different אמוראים with almost the same name. רבה (with a ה) says straw, and רבא (with an א) says cheap barley.

phrases.english: Rava says: the value of barley at a cheap price.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The benefit payment equals the cheapest price of barley.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says each opinion has a ברייתא behind it. רבי שמעון בן יוחי supports רבה: the owner pays only the value of straw.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught that fits רבה, and a ברייתא was taught that fits רבא. The one that fits רבה: רבי שמעון בן יוחי says the owner pays only the value of straw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא announces that both opinions have support. Then it brings the support for רבה first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן יוחי says the owner pays 'only' the value of straw. That is exactly רבה's measure.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא was taught that fits his view

phrases.english: It was taught in line with Rabba,
it was taught in line with Rava.
It was taught in line with Rabba:
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says:
it pays nothing but
the value of straw alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה תַּנְיָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for רבה
steps.raayaObject: רבה's view that the payment is the price of straw
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the court does not charge the full price of what was eaten. It estimates what a person would pay to feed his animal suitable food, even food it does not usually eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught in line with רבא: if the animal benefited, it pays for what it benefited. How so? If it ate one קב or two, we do not say he pays their full value. Rather, we estimate how much a person would pay to feed his animal something fit for it, even if it is not used to that food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא that supports רבא and explains how the benefit is measured.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא measures the benefit by food 'fit for' the animal, 'even if' it is not used to it. That means barley, not just the straw the owner usually gives. The owner does not pay full value either, which matches רבא's 'cheap price.'

keyTerms.meaning: A unit for measuring dry goods like grain
We estimate, the court makes an assessment
Fit for it, suitable food for the animal
Even though it is not used to it

phrases.english: It was taught in line with Rava:
If it benefited, it pays what it benefited.
How so? If it ate a kav or two kav,
we do not say it should pay their value,
rather, we estimate
how much a person would want to spend to feed his animal
something fit for it,
even though it is not used to it.
phrases.notes: This is the key line for רבא. Barley counts even if this animal normally gets only straw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for רבא, parallel to Step 27
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that the payment is the cheap price of barley
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that measures benefit by suitable food, even food the animal is not used to

steps.title: Harmful food means no payment
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא concludes that if the animal ate wheat or something bad for it, the owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, if it ate wheat or something bad for it, it is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא draws a conclusion from its rule. If the food did the animal no good, there was no benefit, so there is nothing to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Payment here is only for benefit, not for the damage. Wheat or harmful food gives the animal no benefit, so in רשות הרבים the owner pays nothing at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Bad for it, harmful to the animal

steps.whatToRemember: In רשות הרבים the owner pays only for what his animal actually gained. רבה says that is the price of straw. רבא says it is barley at the cheapest price. If the animal gained nothing, the owner pays nothing.

phrases.english: Therefore, if it ate wheat
or something bad for it, it is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְפִיכָךְ אָכְלָה חִטִּין אוֹ דָּבָר הָרַע לָהּ פְּטוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion of the ברייתא from Step 28
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Payment follows benefit only. Food that does not benefit the animal, like wheat or harmful food, brings no payment.

steps.title: רב חסדא tells רמי בר חמא about a fine discussion he missed
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא tells רמי בר חמא that he missed a night of excellent questions, and רמי בר חמא asks what they were.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said to רמי בר חמא: You were not with us last night in our area, when we asked about some excellent questions. רמי בר חמא said: What were those excellent questions?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story that sets up a new question. It is preparing us for the question רב חסדא is about to present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is decided here; this is the opening scene. Calling the topic 'excellent matters' tells us the coming question is subtle and worth close attention. It connects to the earlier theme of paying for benefit received.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרָמֵי בַּר חָמָא:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said to Rami bar Chama:
You were not with us at night within the boundary,
phrases.notes: 'The boundary' here means the area where רב חסדא and his group were staying.

phrases.english: when we asked about excellent matters.
He said: What are the excellent matters?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: לָא הֲוֵית גַּבַּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, related to the earlier theme of paying for benefit received.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling. This is a story that introduces the coming question.

steps.title: Must someone who lives in another's courtyard without permission pay rent?
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא presents the question: does a person who lives in his friend's courtyard without permission have to pay rent?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said to him: If someone lives in his friend's courtyard without the owner knowing, does he have to pay him rent, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא states the main question of this new section. Does a squatter owe the owner rent?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether using someone's property without permission creates a duty to pay. The owner never agreed to rent it out, so there was no deal. The question is whether the benefit alone creates a debt.

keyTerms.meaning: One who lives in his friend's courtyard

steps.whyThisMatters: This question becomes the standard source for the rule of זה נהנה וזה לא חסר, which applies to many cases of using someone else's property.

phrases.english: He said to him:
One who lives in his fellow's courtyard without his knowledge –
must he pay him rent,
or does he not need to?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַדָּר בַּחֲצַר חֲבֵירוֹ שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ צָרִיךְ לְהַעֲלוֹת לוֹ שָׂכָר אוֹ אֵין צָרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רמי בר חמא's question by stating the dilemma.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a squatter must pay rent to the owner of the courtyard he lived in without permission.

steps.title: Which case is meant? Not one where nobody gains or loses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the question is about. It cannot be a case where the squatter gains nothing and the owner loses nothing, because then there is obviously no payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it is a courtyard that is not normally rented out, and a man who would not normally pay rent, then this one gained nothing and that one lost nothing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wants to pin down exactly which case the question is about. It tries the first option and shows it is too obvious to ask about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two things could make the squatter owe money: he gained something, or the owner lost something. Here the owner would have left the courtyard empty, and the squatter had somewhere free to stay. With no gain and no loss, he clearly pays nothing, so this cannot be the question.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? (asking for the exact situation)
A man who would not rent (he has free lodging elsewhere)

keyTerms.term: זֶה לֹא נֶהֱנֶה וְזֶה לֹא חָסֵר
keyTerms.meaning: This one does not benefit and that one does not lose

phrases.english: What is the case?
If we say it is a courtyard that does not stand to be rented out,
and a man who would not rent –

phrases.aramaic: זֶה לֹא נֶהֱנֶה וְזֶה לֹא חָסֵר!
phrases.english: this one does not benefit and that one does not lose!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא בְּחָצֵר דְּלָא קָיְימָא לְאַגְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the setting of רב חסדא's dilemma and rules out the first possible case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which exact situation the dilemma is about, given that the simple cases seem obvious.

steps.title: Not a case where one gains and the other loses either
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the opposite case: a courtyard normally rented out, and a man who would have paid rent. That is also obvious, because he gained and the owner lost, so he surely pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say it is a courtyard that is normally rented out, and a man who would normally pay rent. Then this one gained and that one lost, so obviously he must pay!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the second option and shows it is also too obvious. That leaves the question looking pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the owner could have earned rent, and the squatter saved himself rent he would have paid elsewhere. With a gain on one side and a loss on the other, he clearly pays. The challenge is: if both extreme cases are obvious, what was the question?

keyTerms.meaning: A courtyard that stands to be rented out
This one benefits and that one loses: he clearly must pay

phrases.english: Rather, in a courtyard that stands to be rented out,
and a man who would rent –
this one benefits and that one loses!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בְּחָצֵר דְּקָיְימָא לְאַגְרָא, וְגַבְרָא דַּעֲבִיד לְמֵיגַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the challenge: both simple cases have obvious answers.
steps.kashyaTarget: The point of רב חסדא's dilemma, since it seems to have no unclear case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If neither side gains nor loses, he clearly does not pay; if one gains and the other loses, he clearly pays. So no case seems left to ask about.

steps.title: The real case: the squatter gains, but the owner loses nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the question is about the mixed case: the courtyard is not normally rented out, but the man would have paid rent elsewhere. What is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the question is needed for a courtyard that is not normally rented out, and a man who would normally pay rent. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds the case that really is unclear. The squatter benefits, but the owner loses nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This mixed case is what makes the question 'excellent'. The squatter saved rent he would have paid, but the owner gave up no income. This is the case later called זה נהנה וזה לא חסר.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (for this specific case)
This one benefits and that one does not lose: the mixed case

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two sides. Here the squatter is the one who benefits, because he saved rent. The owner is the one who loses nothing, because he would have left the courtyard empty anyway.
steps.whatToRemember: The real question is the case of זה נהנה וזה לא חסר: the squatter gains, but the owner loses nothing.

phrases.english: No, it is needed –
in a courtyard that does not stand to be rented out,
and a man who would rent;
what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא בְּחָצֵר דְּלָא קָיְימָא לְאַגְרָא, וְגַבְרָא דַּעֲבִיד לְמֵיגַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 32 and 33 by finding the unclear middle case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dilemma is about a courtyard not normally rented out, lived in by a man who would otherwise have paid rent: the squatter benefits, but the owner loses nothing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case (לא צריכא): the dilemma is about the mixed case, not either extreme.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both possible cases seemed to have obvious answers, so רב חסדא's dilemma seemed to have no real case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dilemma is about a courtyard not normally rented out, lived in by a man who would otherwise rent: the squatter benefits but the owner loses nothing.

steps.title: The two sides of the question begin
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts laying out both sides. Maybe the squatter can say 'What loss did I cause you?' Or maybe the owner has an answer back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can the squatter say to the owner: 'What loss did I cause you?' Or perhaps the owner can say to him:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out the two possible arguments in the mixed case. The owner's answer continues in the next lines, so this step sets up what comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The squatter's argument is that payment depends on loss, and the owner lost nothing. The 'or perhaps' tells us the owner also has a claim, based on the benefit the squatter received. That claim comes in the next part of the text.

keyTerms.meaning: He can say (he has a valid legal claim)
What loss did I cause you?

phrases.english: Can he say to him: What loss have I caused you?
phrases.notes: This is the squatter talking to the owner: 'You weren't going to rent it out anyway.'

phrases.english: Or perhaps he can say:
phrases.notes: Now the owner is speaking, and his answer continues right after this.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָצֵי אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי חַסַּרְתָּיךְ? אוֹ דִלְמָא, מָצֵי אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the two sides of the dilemma just defined.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the squatter's claim of 'I caused you no loss' frees him from paying, or whether the owner has a valid claim back.
